questions.concept: Vector vs scalar — what the arrow adds
questions.question: Speed is 60 km/h but velocity is 60 km/h north. Why can two objects with equal speed end up in very different places?
questions.solution: Velocity carries DIRECTION; adding displacements requires adding directions, not just magnitudes. Two cars each driving 60 km — one north, one east — end up √(60²+60²) ≈ 85 km apart. A vector's magnitude and direction are both load-bearing; a scalar discards half the information.

questions.question: Given a·b = |a||b|cosθ, why does a·b = 0 certify perpendicularity, and why does the dot product never detect parallel vectors uniquely?
questions.solution: cos 90° = 0, so ANY perpendicular pair gives zero regardless of magnitudes — the dot product is a projection: it measures how much of a lies along b. For parallel vectors cosθ = ±1 and a·b is maximal — but a nonzero value is consistent with any non-perpendicular angle, so only the zero test is conclusive. Projection is the physical meaning.

questions.question: Explain the two pieces of information |a×b| and its direction give, and why the cross product is not commutative.
questions.solution: |a×b| = |a||b|sinθ is the AREA of the parallelogram the two vectors span. Its direction is perpendicular to both (right-hand rule) — the normal of that plane. a×b = −(b×a): flipping the operand order flips the normal's direction, so the product is ANTICOMMUTATIVE. Magnitude = area, direction = orientation of that area.

questions.concept: Unit vector — direction stripped of size
questions.question: Why divide a vector by its own magnitude to get a unit vector, and what does a·â (dot with a unit vector) give you?
questions.solution: â = a/|a| preserves direction but sets the length to 1 — a pure direction indicator. a·â = |a|cosθ is the SCALAR PROJECTION of a onto â's direction: how much of a points that way. Unit vectors turn direction questions into simple dot products.

questions.question: Why does the midpoint of AB have position vector (a+b)/2, and how does the general section formula generalise it?
questions.solution: The midpoint divides AB in ratio 1:1, so r = (1·a + 1·b)/(1+1) = (a+b)/2 — a weighted average of the endpoints. The general internal-division formula r = (mb + na)/(m+n) weights the FAR endpoint more when the division point is closer to it. Averages of position vectors are the vector way to do geometry.

questions.question: Why does [a b c] = 0 certify that three vectors are coplanar?
questions.solution: [a b c] = a·(b×c) is the SIGNED VOLUME of the parallelepiped the three vectors span. Coplanar vectors span a flat figure with zero volume, so the triple product vanishes. Volume zero ⇔ flat ⇔ linearly dependent — the geometric meaning of the determinant test.

questions.question: Why is the work done by a force F over displacement d given by F·d, and when is it zero despite a large force?
questions.solution: Work counts only the force component ALONG the displacement: W = |F||d|cosθ = F·d. If θ = 90° (carrying a bag horizontally, normal force on a level floor), cosθ = 0 and no work is done by that force despite its magnitude. Perpendicular forces do no work — the dot product encodes it automatically.

questions.question: Why does a wrench work best when the force is perpendicular to the handle, and why does pushing along the handle do nothing? Use τ = r × F.
questions.solution: τ = r × F has magnitude |r||F|sinθ — maximal at θ = 90°, zero at θ = 0 (pushing along the handle through the pivot). Only the PERPENDICULAR component of F creates rotation; the direction of τ (along the bolt axis) gives the rotation sense by the right-hand rule. Both magnitude and axis come from the cross product.
